Shed Slabs in Florida: Thickness, Tie-Downs and Permits

A shed slab in Florida is commonly poured 4 in thick, a half-inch above the state's 3½-inch code minimum, with anchor bolts cast in at pour time so the structure can act as one connected unit in high wind. As of October 2026, an 8×8 ft shed faces roughly 2,100 lb of horizontal force in a 130 mph wind, and whether the slab itself needs a permit varies sharply by Florida city and county.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

How Thick Should a Shed Slab Be in Florida?

Four inches is the common built thickness for a shed slab in Florida, a full half-inch above the state's 3½ in code floor for any ground-supported slab, with 3,000 psi concrete and wire mesh or fiber mixed through the pour to hold hairline cracks together rather than prevent them outright (FBC Residential Ch. 5). A heavier metal building or a shed stocked with a riding mower, a generator and shelving loaded with tools can justify stepping up to 5 or 6 in, the same jump a driveway takes once it carries real weight rather than foot traffic. Our concrete slabs page covers the full thickness and reinforcement range across every kind of utility pad.

What Size Pad Does a Shed Need?

A pad is normally cut 6 to 12 in larger than the shed's footprint on every side, enough to keep the structure's sill plate and door threshold off bare soil and to give a mower or a dolly a solid edge to roll onto rather than stepping down into grass or mulch. The concrete slabs page walks through sizing a pad against a specific shed's dimensions once the model and footprint are picked out; this guide focuses on thickness, anchoring and permitting rather than repeating that sizing detail.

Does a Shed Slab Need a Vapor Retarder or Wire Mesh?

Florida's residential code calls for a 6-mil polyethylene sheet under most slabs, with laps of at least 6 in, though it carves out an exception for unheated accessory structures, which covers the overwhelming majority of backyard sheds; wire mesh is standard practice regardless, since it keeps a shrinkage crack from opening into a trip hazard even though it doesn't stop the crack from forming in the first place (FBC Residential Ch. 5). A small slab under about 120 sq ft rarely needs a control joint cut into it the way a driveway panel does, since there's little room for the slab to move before it reaches an edge.

How Do You Anchor a Shed Against Florida Hurricane Wind?

A shed anchored to a concrete slab holds together far better in high wind than one sitting loose on blocks or gravel, since the slab lets the structure act as one connected box instead of a frame that can rack and separate at the corners. The state's own hurricane retrofit guidance puts the problem in concrete terms: an 8 by 8 ft shed in a 130 mph wind faces roughly 2,100 lb of horizontal force, and the guidance recommends anchoring the frame directly to the slab, with screw anchors and crisscrossed straps as the fallback where no slab exists, plus a rope tied around the structure at mid-height as extra restraint (Florida Division of Emergency Management, Hurricane Retrofit Guide). Anchor bolts or straps cast into the slab at the time of the pour, rather than drilled in afterward, give the shed's floor plate a connection that doesn't rely on the concrete's surface alone holding the fastener.

Does a Shed Slab Need a Permit?

It depends heavily on the shed's size and the specific city or county, more than almost any other flatwork question in this guide. Seminole County's non-structural exemption list names sheds of 200 sq ft or less specifically, while its list says nothing about driveways, pavers or other slabs, which shows how size-specific these thresholds get (Seminole County, state legislation affecting permits). Since July 1, 2026, Florida law also exempts single-family owners from a building permit for work valued under $7,500, though the exemption excludes structural work and never reaches a separate zoning or land-development permit a city might still require for a new accessory structure (City of Orlando, HB 803 exemption guide). Because exemption thresholds vary this much by jurisdiction, and several counties in our service areas publish no shed-specific rule at all, calling the local building department before pouring is the only reliable way to know whether a given shed slab needs its own permit.

Gravel Pad or Poured Slab Under a Shed: Does It Matter?

A gravel pad costs less and drains well, but it gives a shed's floor nothing to anchor into beyond what's driven straight into the ground, and it settles unevenly enough over a few wet seasons that doors can bind against their frames. A poured slab costs more upfront and takes longer to cure before the shed can go up, but it gives the structure a continuous, level connection point for anchoring and keeps the floor from settling at a different rate than the walls around it. Most owners planning to keep a shed in place for years, rather than a seasonal or portable unit, find the slab pays for itself in fewer sticking doors and a sturdier anchor point alone.

Say You're Pouring a Pad for a 10×12 Shed in a Central Florida Subdivision

A 10×12 ft shed gets an 11×13 ft pad, 4 in thick with wire mesh, which keeps the slab under most counties' smallest non-structural exemption thresholds where one exists, though that's confirmed with the local building department before the pour rather than assumed. Anchor bolts are set into the wet concrete at the shed manufacturer's bolt pattern, and the pad is graded with a slight slope away from the house so runoff from the shed's roof doesn't pool against the structure's own foundation. Our RV and boat pad guide covers the same base and permitting questions for a larger utility pad on the same lot.

Frequently asked questions

How thick should a shed slab be?

Four inches is the common built thickness, a half-inch above Florida's 3½-inch code floor for any ground-supported slab, with wire mesh or fiber mixed through the pour. A heavier building or a shed loaded with equipment can justify stepping up to 5 or 6 inches.

Does a shed need to be anchored to its slab in Florida?

Anchoring a shed directly to a concrete slab is one of the most effective ways to keep it from racking apart or lifting in high wind, since the slab lets the structure act as one connected unit rather than a loose frame. State hurricane guidance recommends anchor bolts or straps cast into the slab at the time of the pour.

Do I need a permit for a shed slab in Florida?

It depends on the shed's size and the specific city or county; thresholds vary widely. Seminole County, for example, exempts sheds of 200 square feet or less from its non-structural permit list, while other jurisdictions publish no size-specific rule at all. Confirming with the local building department before pouring is the only reliable approach.

Can a shed sit on a gravel pad instead of a poured slab?

It can, and it costs less upfront, but gravel gives a shed's floor nothing solid to anchor into and tends to settle unevenly over time, which can bind doors against their frames. A poured slab holds its level better and gives anchor bolts a continuous connection point.

Does a shed slab need a vapor barrier?

Florida's residential code generally requires a 6-mil poly sheet under slabs, but it carves out an exception for unheated accessory structures, which covers most backyard sheds. Wire mesh is still standard practice regardless, since it keeps a shrinkage crack from opening into a trip hazard.
